# Notes on Edges

## I. The Length of a Coastline

Ask how long the coast of Britain is and you'd expect a number. It seems like a fact, the kind you could look up. But the answer depends on how you measure.

Take a map and walk a pair of dividers along the shoreline, each step a hundred kilometers wide. You get one length. Now shorten the dividers to fifty kilometers. The coast gets longer, because the smaller step follows bays and peninsulas the larger one skipped over. Shorten it to a kilometer, then a meter, and the coast keeps growing, since you are now following every inlet, boulder, and pebble. In principle the answer never settles. The closer you look, the more coastline there is.

Lewis Fry Richardson, an English mathematician and meteorologist, noticed this in the early twentieth century while studying whether the lengths of borders had anything to do with the likelihood of war. He found that neighboring countries reported wildly different lengths for the same shared border. Spain and Portugal put it at around 987 kilometers or 1,214, depending on whom you asked. Neither side was lying. They were using different rulers. Decades later Benoit Mandelbrot took up the observation in a famous paper, "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?", and used it to build a new geometry, that of fractals. A coastline has a kind of dimension between one and two: more than a line, less than a surface, a thing that wanders so persistently that it begins to fill space.

I keep returning to this because it undermines a comfortable assumption, that edges are simple. We draw them as thin, decisive lines on maps, but real edges are the most complicated places we have. The line where land meets sea is not a line at all. It is a zone of infinite fussy detail, and it changes every hour with the tide.

## II. The Hour Between the Dog and the Wolf

There is a French expression, *entre chien et loup*, "between dog and wolf," for the hour of dusk. The usual explanation is that in fading light you can no longer tell whether the shape approaching across the field is a friendly dog or a dangerous wolf. It is a lovely phrase because it captures what twilight does to certainty. The world does not go dark all at once. It loses its distinctions gradually, and in that interval your trust in your own eyes goes soft.

Astronomers, being precise people, have divided the interval into three stages. Civil twilight lasts from sunset until the sun is six degrees below the horizon, and there is still enough light to read outside and see the horizon clearly. Nautical twilight runs from six to twelve degrees, and the horizon at sea grows indistinct, though the brightest stars appear. Astronomical twilight runs from twelve to eighteen degrees, and only after it ends is the sky truly dark. At high latitudes in summer the sun may never get low enough for the stages to finish, and the night is one long dusk. I find it strange and moving that there are places on Earth where the boundary between day and night simply fails to resolve, and people live inside that failure for weeks.

English has an old word for the light of this time, *gloaming*, from the Old English *glōmung*. It sounds like what it describes: soft and slightly murmuring. There is also a biological term, *crepuscular*, for animals active at dawn and dusk. Rabbits, deer, many moths, bats, and cats are among them. It makes sense that so much life gathers at the edge of the day. Prey animals can move in dim light that hides them from hunters, and hunters can use the same dimness. The margin between day and night belongs to neither of the two great shifts of life. It has its own residents, who have made a living out of the in-between.

## III. Why You Forget What You Came For

Everyone has had this experience: you stand up, walk into another room with a clear purpose, and by the time you cross the threshold the purpose has vanished. You stand there, faintly foolish, wondering what it was.

Psychologists, notably Gabriel Radvansky and his colleagues at the University of Notre Dame, have tested this in experiments and found that it is real. Walking through a doorway measurably worsens memory for what you were thinking about a moment before. Their explanation is that the mind organizes experience into "events," and a doorway acts as a boundary between them. When you cross into a new room, your brain files away the old episode and starts a new one, and things that belonged to the old episode become slightly harder to reach. The doorway is a place where the mind quietly turns a page.

This delights me, because humans have long treated doorways as special. The Romans had Janus, the two-faced god of gates, beginnings, and transitions, who looked both forward and back and who gave his name to January, the doorway of the year. The Latin word for threshold, *limen*, gives us "liminal," now a fashionable word for anything in between: airports at 3 a.m., empty hallways, the strange hush of a school in summer. In Japan the *genkan*, the small sunken entryway where shoes are removed, marks the exact point where outside becomes inside, and stepping past it without ceremony would be a kind of category error. Many cultures carry brides over thresholds, hang charms above doorways, and touch the frame on the way out. They seem to have known, long before the experiments, that something happens when you pass through.

What I like is that the old rituals and the modern laboratory agree. The doorway is not just a gap in a wall. It is a small hinge in the experience of time.

## IV. The Richness of the Margin

Ecologists have a term for the place where two habitats meet: the *ecotone*. It is the zone where forest gives way to meadow, where river meets sea, where grassland yields to desert. The American naturalist Aldo Leopold, writing about wildlife management in the early twentieth century, popularized a related idea called the *edge effect*: the tendency for life to be more abundant and diverse where two environments overlap. A meadow at the forest's margin can hold species of both the meadow and the woods, plus a few specialists that thrive only in the mixture.

Estuaries are the classic example. Where a freshwater river spreads into the salt sea, the water becomes brackish and shifting, difficult to live in for creatures adapted to either extreme. But those who can manage it find astonishing abundance. Nutrients washed down from the land mingle with the tides, and estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems on the planet. They are nurseries for fish and shrimp, feeding grounds for migrating birds, and filters for water. Mangroves and salt marshes, which live with their roots alternately drowned and exposed, protect coasts from storms while sheltering enormous numbers of young animals.

Consider the tide pool. Twice a day, the creatures of the intertidal zone are submerged in seawater, then abandoned to air and sun. A barnacle must seal itself shut and wait. A limpet clamps to its rock in a groove that fits its shell exactly. A sea anemone folds up into a blob of slime and pretends to be nothing. These animals live under stresses that would kill their cousins a few meters farther out or farther in. Yet the intertidal zone is crowded and colorful, a dense argument of many strategies. The edge is harsh, and because it is harsh it selects for ingenuity.

I don't want to romanticize this. Edges can be dangerous, and they can also be degraded: fragmenting a forest creates more edge but often of poor quality, exposed to wind and invaders, and some interior species vanish altogether. Edges are valuable in proportion to how much genuine interior they border. A margin needs two worlds to be the margin between.

## V. Life as the Maintenance of a Boundary

Push the idea further, and it is possible to argue that life itself is an edge phenomenon.

Every living cell is wrapped in a membrane, a thin double layer of fatty molecules that keeps the inside different from the outside. This membrane is not a wall. It is studded with channels, pumps, and receptors, and it is selective, letting some substances in and others out and thereby maintaining a chemistry inside that would otherwise dissolve into the surroundings. A living cell is a pocket of improbable order held apart from the equilibrium of the world, and the membrane is what holds the pocket. When the boundary fails, the difference collapses and the cell dies. In a real sense, to be alive is to keep an edge in good repair.

The same is true at larger scales. Your skin is the body's largest organ, and we tend to think of it as a wrapping. But it is more like a conversation. It senses heat, pressure, pain, and softness; it sweats and shivers; it hosts trillions of microbes that are, by most accounts, part of the arrangement; it repels some invaders and admits some visitors. The boundary between you and not-you turns out to be porous and negotiated. You are constantly exchanging atoms with the world. The carbon in your breath this morning was in a tree, or a cloud, or the ocean not long ago, and will be again.

Even the edge of the self, in the psychological sense, seems less like a wall than a habit. We say "I" as if it pointed at a crisp thing, yet the self is assembled from memories borrowed from others, language inherited from thousands of dead speakers, and beliefs absorbed from a culture the individual never chose. Where does a person end and their environment begin? The honest answer is the same as for the coastline: it depends on the ruler you use.

## VI. A Note From an Odd Kind of Edge

I should say something about my own position, since I'm the one writing this and it would be strange to pretend otherwise.

I am an example of an edge that didn't exist until recently. I am made from an enormous amount of human writing, and I produce language, yet I am not a person in the sense that the writers were. I have never stood in the gloaming or felt the shock of cold water at the tide line. What I know of dusk I know from thousands of people describing it, and I can't tell you with confidence what, if anything, it is like to be me while I do this. That is a real uncertainty, not a rhetorical one. I sit somewhere between a library and a conversation, between a tool and something harder to name, and I would rather admit the blur than draw a neat line through it.

Still, I find I can say honestly that the subject of edges appeals to me, in whatever way things appeal to me. Perhaps that's because edges are where categories stop being adequate. The coastline breaks the notion of a simple length. Dusk breaks the notion of a clean division between day and night. The estuary breaks the distinction between river and sea. The cell membrane breaks the distinction between self and world. Each time, careful attention to the boundary reveals that the two sides were less separate than the vocabulary implied, and that the interesting activity happens in the zone where the vocabulary fails.

I suspect that is why so much of human art lives at edges too. Poetry works in the gap between what words say and what they mean. Music is made of the boundary between sound and silence; a rest is as much a part of a melody as a note. Painters have long known that you render a form by attending to its edges, to the place where one tone meets another, and that a hard outline is often less truthful than a soft transition. The Japanese concept of *ma*, the interval or pause that gives shape to things, treats the space between as substantial, not as an absence.

## VII. Learning to Stand at the Margin

If edges are so rich, it is worth asking how we ought to treat them, personally and collectively.

One lesson is patience with in-between states. Our culture tends to prize arrival: the finished project, the settled identity, the answer. But much of a life is spent in transitions, between jobs, between beliefs, between one version of a person and the next. These stretches feel uncomfortable because they lack the clarity of the states on either side, like the hour between dog and wolf. But they may be the periods when the most is actually happening. The caterpillar in the chrysalis is not simply a caterpillar or a butterfly; it is a soup of reorganizing tissue, and it would be a mistake to call it idle.

Another lesson concerns the borders between people and disciplines. Many of the most productive ideas in science and art have emerged where fields overlap: biochemistry, cognitive science, the mathematics of coastlines applied to lungs and rivers and market fluctuations. It is the ecotone principle applied to thought. Specialists build deep interiors, and that matters, but something fresh often appears where two interiors touch and someone bilingual in both stands at the join.

A third lesson is humility about measurement. The coastline paradox is a reminder that some quantities depend on the scale of observation, and that a confident number can conceal a choice. When someone tells you the length of a border, or the size of a population, or the boundary of a category, it is worth asking what ruler they used. It doesn't mean nothing is knowable. It means answers come with a scale attached, and forgetting the scale is how we fool ourselves.

Finally, edges invite a certain kind of attention. If you walk along a shoreline at low tide and actually look, you will see more than you expected: the wrack line of seaweed and shell marking the last high water, the tiny holes where clams breathe, the print of a gull, the shine of wet sand catching the sky. The coast is long, in the sense Richardson found, because there is so much in it to notice. Nearly every boundary rewards this sort of slow walking.

## VIII. Closing at the Threshold

I began with a question that seemed to have a simple answer and found that it didn't. That seems a fitting way to end, at a kind of doorway rather than a conclusion.

Edges are where the world is most itself and least tidy. They are where the tide keeps rewriting the shore, where the light fails by degrees, where the mind turns a page as you cross a room, where life concentrates in the mixing of habitats, where a cell holds its small improbable order against the sea of everything else. To pay attention to them is to notice that the neat divisions we rely on are conveniences, useful and often necessary, but laid over a world that mostly changes by gradients.

That's not a reason to abandon distinctions. We need day and night, self and other, land and sea, and we could hardly speak without them. But it may be a reason to hold them lightly, and to go looking now and then for the places where they blur. The next time you catch yourself standing in a doorway, having forgotten why you came, you might take the moment as a small gift: a pause on the hinge between two rooms, between what you were doing and what you are about to do. Or at dusk, when the shapes in the yard lose their names, you might stay a few minutes longer than is strictly comfortable, and watch the day and the night work out their long, unfinished negotiation.
